``` {r message = F, warning = F}
# Load packages
library(tidyverse) # tidyverse includes ggplot2

# STEP 1: Loading the data

# Import the original CSV files
covar <- read_csv("../Data/GSE85307_covar.csv")
gene_expr <- read_csv("../Data/GSE85307_geneExpression.csv")
gene_names <- read_csv("../Data/GSE85307_geneNames.csv")
```

For our final submission, from a data cleaning and wrangling point of view, we 
need to select 10 genes (we already selected 3 in Submission 2) for our heatmap 
and 2 additional continuous covariates for our summary statistics table.

So, before we do any plotting, like in the previous submissions, we will first 
focus on the data cleaning and wrangling steps.

We will begin by first inspecting the datasets again and then identifying first 
the additional genes (7) that we will use for our heatmap analysis. Once, we have
selected our 10 genes, we will clean up the data and prepare it such that it can 
be used for our analyses. After this, we will also then identify 2 additional
continuous covariates for our summary statistics table. We will then finally begin
the plotting and analysis steps of the project.

### Initial Data Inspection
```{r}

# STEP 2: Inspecting the data

# Checking how many rows and columns are there in each file
dim(covar)      # RESULT: 157 X 10
dim(gene_expr)  # RESULT: 500 X 158
dim(gene_names) # RESULT: 750 X 2

# Checking what the column names are
#names(covar)
#names(gene_expr)  # column names seem to match the geoID in covar
#names(gene_names) # contains a Probe ID and Name....will likely use this probe ID
# to match gene expression with gene name...gene expression columns seem to be 
# like probe ID

# Viewing a few rows of each dataset
#head(covar)
#head(gene_expr[,1:6]) # looking at first 6 columns
#head(gene_names)

# Viewing each dataset fully
#View(covar)
#View(gene_expr)
#View(gene_names)

```
In Submission 2, we selected the genes NFYC, SOCS5, and HAUS4. For Submission 3, 
we now need to select 7 additional genes. 

As a reminder, the gene name dataset contains the gene names and their 
corresponding probe IDs, while the gene expression dataset contains the expression 
values associated with those probe IDs. 

Following what we did in Submission 2, we will again select our 7 additional genes 
by looking at genes which are present in both the gene name data set and the gene 
expression dataset.So this mean that the probe ids for the genes should be present 
in both the datasets (i.e., in the PROBEID column of gene names dataset and in 
the ...1 column of the gene expression dataset)
```{r}
# STEP 3: Identifying genes available in both datasets and picking 7 more (in 
# addition to NFYC, SOCS5, and HAUS4)

# Finding gene names whose probe IDs are also present in the gene expression 
# dataset
availableGenes <- gene_names[gene_names$PROBEID %in% gene_expr$...1, ]

# Looking at some of these genes 
head(availableGenes, 30)
```

So, the 7 additional genes I will pick are CNR1, PTX3, GBX2, BRDT, TRIM24, 
CASC3 and MTMR4.

Now that I have picked the 7 additional genes, I will need to extract the 
expression values for all the ten genes (NFYC, SOCS5, and HAUS4 + CNR1, PTX3, 
GBX2, BRDT, TRIM24, CASC3 and MTMR4) from the gene expression dataset. I will 
then combine these expression values with the covariate dataset so that I can look 
at how the expression of each gene relates to the same maternal characteristics.

I will begin this process by first making the specific gene name + probeID dataset
followed by then joining this with the gene expression info for the genes and then
joining it with the covariate data for these genes.

### Creating our 10 gene-specific dataset
```{r}
# STEP 4: Creating specific gene name + probe ID dataset

# Creating a list of the 10 selected genes
selectedGenes <- c("NFYC", "SOCS5", "HAUS4", 
                   "CNR1", "PTX3", "GBX2", "BRDT", "TRIM24", "CASC3", "MTMR4")

# Identifying and storing probe IDs + names corresponding to the 10 selected 
# genes
selectedGenesInfo <- availableGenes[availableGenes$GENE %in% selectedGenes, ]

# Viewing some of the selected genes and their corresponding probe IDs
#head(selectedGenesInfo)
```

Since the gene expression dataset has probe IDs in its first column and sample 
IDs as the remaining column names, I will use probe IDs to extract the expression
values for each gene (so by selecting specific rows). 
```{r}
# STEP 5: Creating a dataset consisting of expression values for the selected 
# genes

# Selecting the expression data
selectedGeneExpr <- gene_expr[gene_expr$...1 %in% selectedGenesInfo$PROBEID, ]

# Adding in the gene names
selectedGeneExpr <- selectedGeneExpr %>% 
  left_join(selectedGenesInfo, by = c("...1" = "PROBEID"))

# selectedGeneExpr # Looks good! but gene name is in the last column...we will
# change that using relocate [https://dplyr.tidyverse.org/reference/relocate.html]

selectedGeneExpr <- selectedGeneExpr %>%
  relocate(GENE, .after = ...1) # much better!

# selectedGeneExpr # Looks good!
```

Now, we will reshape the data and convert from wide -> long format
```{r}
# STEP 6: Reshaping gene expression data from wide to long format

# Convert the expression data from wide format to long format, and also removing
# the probe ID column since we don't need that anymore
selectedGeneExprLong <- selectedGeneExpr %>%
  pivot_longer(cols = -c(...1, GENE),
               names_to = "geoID",
               values_to = "Expression") %>%
  select(GENE, geoID, Expression)

# Viewing the reshaped data
# head(selectedGeneExprLong) # Looks good!

```

Now, we will join in the covariate info.
```{r}
# STEP 7: Joining gene expression data with covariate data
selectedGeneExprLong <- selectedGeneExprLong %>%
  left_join(covar, by = "geoID")

# Viewing the combined dataset
# head(selectedGeneExprLong) # Looks good!
```

Now, we will reshape the data so that each gene has its own expression column.
```{r}
# STEP 8: Long -> Wide so that each gene has its own expression column

selectedGeneExprWide <- selectedGeneExprLong %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = GENE,
              values_from = Expression) 

# Viewing the now wide dataset
# head(selectedGeneExprWide) # looks good! gene expression data is added to the 
# end so last 10 columns have gene expression data. [also we have 20 columns 
# which is as expected since covar had 10 columns and then we added 10 columns  
# for our 10 genes so 20 makes sense]

```

So, now that we have selected our 10 genes and created a dataset containing the 
information for them, we will clean our data again like we did in the previous
submissions after which we will do one final step of deciding which covariates 
we will be using for plotting and for our summary statistics table.

### Cleaning the Data
```{r}
# STEP 9: Cleaning the data by checking for any missing values, duplicates, etc.

# Checking the no. of missing values in each column
colSums(is.na(selectedGeneExprWide)) # RESULT: 0 for all columns which means that 
# there are no NAs present in our dataset.

# Checking for duplicated rows
sum(duplicated(selectedGeneExprWide)) # RESULT: 0 which means that there are no 
# duplicated rows

# Checking for duplicate sample IDs
sum(duplicated(selectedGeneExprWide$geoID)) # RESULT: 0 which means that there are 
# no duplicated sample IDS

```

Now that we have checked that there are no NAs and duplicated rows, we will now
focus on cleaning up the column values.
```{r}
# STEP 10: Cleaning up the columns

# Taking a look at the data again so that we know what to put down for our mutate()
#head(selectedGeneExprWide)

# Creating a copy so our new genes dataset remains unchanged
cleanGenesData <- selectedGeneExprWide

# Removing descriptive labels (using gsub) and converting to numerical variables 
# where appropriate (using as.numeric())
cleanGenesData <- cleanGenesData %>%
  mutate(
    # Removing both descriptive labels and converting to numeric (so it is treated 
    # as such)
    mat_age_yrs = as.numeric(gsub("age_years: ",
                                  "", mat_age_yrs)),
    delivery_gestAge_wks = as.numeric(gsub("gestation_weeks: ", 
                                           "", delivery_gestAge_wks)),
    sampleCollection_gestAge_wks = as.numeric(gsub("blood_draw_at_gestation_week: ", 
                                                   "", sampleCollection_gestAge_wks)),
    mat_BMI = as.numeric(gsub("bmi_kg/m2: ", 
                              "", mat_BMI)),  
    # because parentheses are not treated as literal characters and are treated 
    # specially in regular expressions, we add \\ to them so that R treats them 
    # as being literal parentheses.
    mat_vitD = as.numeric(gsub("vitamind_25\\(0h\\)_ng/ml_whole_blood_baseline: ", 
                               "", mat_vitD)),          

    # Only removing descriptive labels
    preg_preeclampsia = gsub("pregnancy_condition: ","", preg_preeclampsia),
    batch_Microarray = gsub("microarray_hybridization_date: ", "", batch_Microarray),
    
    # Removing descriptive labeling and converting 0 to Healthy and 1 to Asthmatic
    mat_asthma = gsub("asthma_0=healthy_1=asthmatic: ", "", mat_asthma),
    mat_asthma = ifelse(mat_asthma=="0", "Healthy", "Asthmatic"))

# Creating vitamin D groups using 20 ng/mL as the cutoff.
# I selected this cutoff after researching commonly used reference thresholds.
# Reference: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK532266/
cleanGenesData <- cleanGenesData %>% 
  mutate(mat_vitD_group = factor(ifelse(mat_vitD < 20, 
                                        "Below 20 ng/mL", 
                                        "20 ng/mL or above"),
                                 levels = c("Below 20 ng/mL", 
                                            "20 ng/mL or above")))

#head(cleanGenesData) # Looks good! but VitaminD group is in the last column...
# we will change that using relocate 
# [https://dplyr.tidyverse.org/reference/relocate.html]
cleanGenesData <- cleanGenesData %>%
  relocate(mat_vitD_group, .after = mat_vitD)

# Taking a look at our data to see if it looks good. 
#head(cleanGenesData) # RESULT: Looks good! Much neater and cleaner.
```
Now that we have cleaned up within the columns, we will do another check to see 
if there is any missing data, i.e., if anything became NA. If we did it 
correctly, we will see no NA values because our dataset didn't have any NA values 
to begin with.

```{r}
# STEP 11: Verifying that we don't have any missing values after cleaning 

# Checking the no. of missing values in each column
colSums(is.na(cleanGenesData)) # RESULT: 0 for all columns which means that there 
# are no NAs present in our dataset.

```
Great, there is no missing data in our cleaned dataset so our dataset is now ready 
to be used for analysis.

Before, we delve into analysis, we need to select our 2 additional continuous 
covariates. As a reminder, from our previous submissions, the covariates we 
selected were as follows: 
- Continuous Covariate: Maternal age ("mat_age_yrs")
- First Categorical Covariate: Pregnancy condition ("preg_preeclampsia")
- Second Categorical Covariate: Maternal Vitamin D group ("mat_vitD_group"; 
                                                           from "mat_vitD")
                                                           
The 2 additional continuous covariates we will use are 1. maternal BMI ("mat_BMI")
and 2. gestational age at delivery in weeks("delivery_gestAge_wks").

We also need our summary statistics table to be stratified by a categorical 
covariate which we will choose to be the pregnancy condition.

Okay, now that we selected the covariates as well, the next step is analysis, which
we will do by 1. plotting our 3 selected genes from Submission 2, 2. making our
summary statistics table, 3. making our heatmap and 4. making our additional plot
which we will choose to be a lollipop plot.

### Analysis

Before, we make our plotting function, we will create our very own custom theme 
that will be used for the plotting
```{r}
# STEP 12: Making the custom theme for the plots

library(ggplot2)

# Here to create my own custom theme, I am making a dark background theme with 
# the axes and text in white. The legend is placed at the bottom. We will also 
# remove all the extra border and grid lines to make it look cleaner.
newBlackTheme <- theme( 
  
  # Remove all the extra borders and grid lines
  panel.border = element_blank(),     # remove the borders 
  panel.grid.major = element_blank(), # removes the major grid lines
  panel.grid.minor = element_blank(), # removes the minor grid lines
  
  # Sets the axis color and text to white
  axis.line = element_line(color="white"),               # sets axis line color to white
  axis.text = element_text(colour = "white", size = 12), # sets axis text to white
  axis.ticks = element_line(colour = "white"),           # sets axis tick to white
  
  # Sets plot background to black
  plot.background = element_rect(fill = "black"), # this sets background color to black
  panel.background = element_blank(),             # this removes the panel background

  # This centers the plot title
  plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5, size = 13),
  
  # Sets text color to white
  text = element_text(colour = "white", size = 12),
  
  # Sets legend color as black
  legend.key = element_rect(fill = "black"), # this sets legend key background to black
  legend.background = element_rect(fill = "black"), # this sets legend background to black
  
  # Sets legend text color as white
  legend.text = element_text(colour = "white", size = 12),
  legend.title = element_text(colour = "white", size = 12),
  
  # Sets legend position to bottom
  legend.position = "bottom")  

```


```{r}
# STEP 13: Making the plotting function

# Inputs:
# df: cleaned dataset
# genes: list of gene names
# continuousCovariate: name of the continuous covariate
# categoricalCovariates: names of the two categorical covariates

# Setting common axis limits across all three genes

makeGenePlots <- function(df, genes, continuousCovariate, categoricalCovariates){
  
  # I am setting common axis limits across all three genes so that their plots 
  # can be compared more easily and any differences we observe visually are not 
  # exaggerated by differences in axis scales. We use range() to get both min. and
  # max. values. We also use unlist() so that the 3 gene columns are combined into 
  # one vector. Later on when plotting, we use coord_cartesian() so that the x/y 
  # limits can be applied to our plots.
  
  expressionLimits <- range(unlist(df[genes]), na.rm = TRUE) # Finding min. and 
  # and max. expression values across the 3 gene expression columns
  
  ageLimits <- range(df[[continuousCovariate]], na.rm = TRUE) # Finding min. and 
  # max. values of maternal age (continuous covariate)
  
  # Looping through each gene
  for (gene in genes){
    
    # Creating a histogram for each selected gene
    histPlot <- ggplot(df, aes(x = .data[[gene]])) + # we use .data[[gene]] so 
      # that the function knows which column to use in the dataframe specified
      # since our gene expression data is stored under its gene name, we just have
      # to specify the gene
      geom_histogram(bins = 20, fill = "darkgreen", color = "white") +
      labs(title = paste("Distribution of", gene, "Expression"),
           x = paste(gene, "Expression"),
           y = "Number of Samples") +
      coord_cartesian(xlim = expressionLimits, ylim = c(0,30)) + # applying limits
      # to both axes
      newBlackTheme
    
    print(histPlot)
    
    # Creating a scatterplot for each selected gene [x = continuous covariate; 
    # y = gene expression]...I have also added a line of best here
    scatterPlot <- ggplot(df, aes(x = .data[[continuousCovariate]],
                                  y = .data[[gene]])) +
      geom_point(color = "#B2FBA5", size = 1.5, alpha = 0.6) +
      
      geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = TRUE, 
                  color = "white", linewidth = 0.6) + # line of best fit, to better
      # assess the relationship of the data for a scatterplot
      
      labs(title = paste(gene, "Expression vs. Maternal Age"),
           x = "Maternal Age (Years)",
           y = paste(gene, "Expression")) +
      coord_cartesian(xlim = ageLimits, ylim = expressionLimits) + # applying 
      # limits to both axes
      newBlackTheme
    
    print(scatterPlot)
    
    # Creating a boxplot for each selected gene 
    boxPlot <- ggplot(df, aes(x = .data[[categoricalCovariates[1]]],
                              y = .data[[gene]], 
                              color = .data[[categoricalCovariates[2]]])) +
      geom_boxplot(fill = "black", width = 0.7,
                   position = position_dodge(width = 0.85), # because jitter points 
                   # are overlapping
                   outlier.shape = NA) +
      geom_jitter(position = position_jitterdodge(jitter.width = 0.15, 
                                                  dodge.width = 0.85),
                  alpha = 0.6, size = 1.5) +
      scale_color_manual(values = c("#E5A9FF", "#00FF00")) +
      labs(title = paste(gene, "Expression by Pregnancy Condition and Vitamin D Group"),
           x = "Pregnancy Condition",
           y = paste(gene, "Expression"),
           color =" Vitamin D Group") +
      coord_cartesian(ylim = expressionLimits) + # applying y axis limits
      newBlackTheme
    
    print(boxPlot)
  }
}
```

Let's now run this function:  

The variables we will use for plotting are as follows:
- Genes of Interest: NFYC, SOCS5, HAUS4 ("selectedGenes")
- Continous Covariate: Maternal age ("mat_age_yrs")
- First Categorical Covariate: Pregnancy condition ("preg_preeclampsia")
- Second Categorical Covariate: Maternal Vitamin D group ("mat_vitD_group"; 
                                                           from "mat_vitD")
                                                           
```{r}
# STEP 14: Running the plotting function with common axis limits

threeGenes <- c("NFYC", "SOCS5", "HAUS4")

makeGenePlots(df = cleanGenesData, 
              genes = threeGenes,
              continuousCovariate = "mat_age_yrs",
              categoricalCovariates = c("preg_preeclampsia", "mat_vitD_group"))

```
Now, that we have generated the 9 plots like we did in Submission 2, we will now
focus on making our summary statistics table.

For our summary statistics table, we want to do it for 3 continuous covariates 
and 2 categorical covariates, stratified by a categorical covariate. As mentioned
earlier, we will stratify the table using the categorical covariate, pregnancy
condition.

So to summarize, the covariates we will choose for our table is as follows: 
- First Continuous Covariate: Maternal age ("mat_age_yrs")
- Second Continuous Covariate: Maternal BMI ("mat_BMI")
- Three Continuous Covariate: Gestational age at delivery in weeks 
  ("delivery_gestAge_wks")

- First Categorical Covariate: Pregnancy condition ("preg_preeclampsia");
  will use this for stratifying the table
- Second Categorical Covariate: Maternal Vitamin D group ("mat_vitD_group"; 
                                                           from "mat_vitD")
